transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-05-21 14:00 PT
Duration: 54 mins
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Luis Ramirez (Horizon CTO), Priya Singh (Lead ML Eng), Tom Becker (Platform)

Auto-generated Summary:
Quick hosted API demo focusing on chat/text generation basics: streaming behavior, parameter tuning (temperature/top_p/max_tokens), retry and idempotency patterns, and how Redwood Optimize/Console suggests batching/caching to reduce cost. Customer concerned about latency (mobile use case), data residency, and how to run a short benchmark.

Topics:
- Streaming semantics (SSE vs websockets), chunk boundaries, reassembly
- Idempotency keys + retries, exponential backoff and jitter
- Parameters: temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop, system vs user messages
- Console: per-route latency, token-cost breakdown, Optimize suggestions (batching, KV/prefix cache, quantization hints)
- Fallbacks & routing: smaller model variants, regional routing, dedicated pool vs hosted tradeoffs
- Security/compliance brief: SOC 2, KMS, audit logs

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan, AE on the account, and Maya is our solutions engineer. We're gonna walk through the hosted gen API, how streaming behaves, and some practical retry patterns — keep it hands-on.
[00:18] Luis: Great, thanks. We're mostly interested in mobile chat so latency is key, um, and cost. We want to see how Redwood handles streaming and any edge cases where a user sees partial responses.
[00:32] Maya: Totally. We'll start with the streaming model. Redwood supports chunked streaming over Server-Sent Events and websockets depending on your client. The important bit is that we emit tokens/chunks frequently so the client can render partial text. Occasionally the transcript will show artifacts — like token-level splits — so you want to do reassembly on our delimiters.
[00:55] Priya: When you say delimiters, you mean the delta chunks that include text and role? How do we know when a chunk is complete?
[01:05] Maya: Good question. Each chunk contains a small JSON delta with a sequence index. We recommend clients buffer until the chunk completes, but also show streaming tokens as they arrive. For mobile, we usually render partial strings — but avoid showing half a word by waiting for whitespace or punctuation or by merging small trailing fragments.
[01:28] Tom: Are there any guarantees around ordering? If we reconnect do we risk getting duplicates?
[01:36] Maya: Ordering is preserved per connection. For reconnections, we surface a resume token in the stream if the client reconnects within a short window — think 30 seconds — otherwise it's a fresh response. That resume path is experimental and has caveats; most teams implement idempotency and retry guards client-side.
[01:55] Jordan: On that note, retrying -- we always advise using a request_id or idempotency key so retries for the same user action are deduped server-side. Use exponential backoff with jitter, start at ~200ms, cap around 5s for user-facing flows. For heavy background batch jobs we use longer windows.
[02:20] Priya: So if a mobile app sees a timeout and retries, how does Redwood avoid double-charging tokens or generating two outputs?
[02:29] Maya: Token billing is tied to completed requests. If a retry uses the same idempotency key and the original completed, we return the stored response and do not re-run model compute. If it didn't complete, the retry will run but dedupe logic tries to keep duplicate generations minimal. There's a small window where duplicates are possible if two retries race and neither reached persistence yet — that's the race condition you referenced.
[02:54] Luis: That race condition is a concern because our UX analytics will consider duplicates as new messages.
[03:01] Jordan: Right — product workaround is to include a client-side dedupe by matching server response hashes or message ids. Also Redwood's Console provides token-level and request-level logs so you can filter duplicates in analytics.
[03:18] Maya: Moving on to params: temperature controls randomness, top_p is nucleus sampling. For deterministic generation (e.g., policy answers) we recommend temperature 0.0 and low top_p. For creative text we'll show 0.7–0.9. Max_tokens is enforced server-side; you can configure output length budgets per route in the Console.
[03:41] Priya: Any advice on stop sequences and partial streaming? Sometimes stop tokens arrive mid-chunk.
[03:49] Maya: We emit a final chunk that indicates 'finished' with stop reason. Clients should treat that final chunk as authoritative. If stop arrives mid-chunk, the chunk contains a truncated text and a finished flag. Again, small transcription noise possible.
[04:06] Tom: What's the best pattern for short latencies — e.g., wanting 200–300ms p95 on responses for 8–16 token replies?
[04:15] Maya: For very short replies, we recommend: 1) pin to a low-latency model family; 2) use prefix caching (if many chats share the same system prompt) — Redwood's KV/prefix cache caches key-value state and reduces autoregression compute; 3) set small max_tokens and a short timeout; 4) enable batching-aware paths on the client so small requests can be consolidated server-side where beneficial.
[04:42] Priya: Prefix cache — will that store user messages? Any PII concerns?
[04:47] Jordan: By default prefix caching stores non-sensitive prefixes; for any PII you can opt out. For Private or Dedicated deployments you can configure the cache retention or disable it. All cached artifacts respect your data retention policy and KMS settings for encryption at rest.
[05:03] Luis: We also need SOC 2 and audit logs. Does Console surface request-level audit trails?
[05:11] Jordan: Yes, we have audit logs for all request metadata and an enterprise log export for SIEM. SOC 2 is supported; we have an AICPA report and you can use our KMS integration to manage keys. We'll attach the security pack in the follow-up.
[05:25] Maya: Now on retries: implement exponential backoff with jitter and a maximum retry count. For streaming, if you get transient network errors, reconnect and resume if available, otherwise re-run the request with the same idempotency key. If you see 429s, consider client-side throttling and also the Console's per-route rate dashboards to tune quotas.
[05:46] Priya: How aggressive should we be with retries on mobile networks?
[05:49] Maya: Mobile is tricky. Short retries (200–500ms) with a low max attempts (2–3) for interactive flows is common. For background tasks you can be more persistent. Also leverage local heuristics: if signal is poor, defer heavy requests or batch them.
[06:04] Tom: Can Redwood automatically fall back to a smaller cheaper model when capacity is constrained?
[06:09] Jordan: Yes — routing policies can be set per-route. We support graceful fallback to verified smaller variants when higher-tier models are unavailable. There's a cost/quality tradeoff; Console shows expected quality delta and cost impact per fallback.
[06:24] Luis: About Console and Optimize — how prescriptive are Optimize suggestions? It flagged batching and quantization earlier when we trialed the demo account.
[06:33] Maya: Optimize runs lightweight telemetry on token distribution and recommends batching windows, cache keys, and quantization profiles. For example it might recommend int8 quantization for certain models to reduce inference cost with minimal quality impact. These are recommendations; you can apply them via the Console or via our API.
[06:51] Priya: Any sample numbers for cost gains from batching + caching?
[06:55] Maya: Rough numbers: small interactive workloads with 50–80% repeated prefixes see 20–40% token compute reduction from prefix caching. Batching improves throughput for parallel requests and can cut per-token cost by 10–30% depending on utilization. Quantization can cut model memory and often reduces cost by 20–50% on dedicated pools. We'll include a short spreadsheet in the follow-up.
[07:19] Jordan: Quick demo time — we'll do a cURL + Node example. (screen sharing) Here's a minimal request: POST /v1/chat with messages array, set stream=true to get SSE chunks, include x-idempotency-key header.
[07:38] Maya: Note: when using SDKs we provide helpers that rebuild partial messages and surface a single callback for 'delta' vs 'complete' chunks. If you're rolling a custom client, try to capture sequence ids and merge.
[07:53] Priya: We're concerned with analytics — how to map streaming deltas to a single message id downstream?
[07:59] Maya: Each completed response includes a message_id and a request_id. Use message_id as canonical and attach it to analytics events when final chunk arrives. For partial renders, you can emit intermediate UI events but mark them provisional.
[08:14] Tom: Any limits on concurrent streams per API key?
[08:18] Jordan: By default there's a per-account concurrency soft limit; you can request higher concurrency for production and we can provision via Dedicated or reserved capacity. Console shows per-key concurrency and you can set quotas.
[08:32] Luis: For the pilot we want to run 1,000 daily active users with 200 RPS peak bursts, mostly short replies.
[08:40] Maya: That sounds reasonable. We'll propose a dedicated throughput plan if you need strict p95 latency SLAs; otherwise the hosted tier with routing and caching often meets mobile p95s for short replies.
[08:53] Priya: Any gotchas about streaming and mobile backgrounding? If app goes to background we lose socket — how to resume?
[08:59] Maya: Best practice is to cancel and re-render with same idempotency key on resume; treat partial responses as transient. If resume tokens are available within the short window, you can attempt it but fallback to re-request is the reliable path.
[09:14] Jordan: Security quick note — for Private deployments we can ship an on-prem package, and for VPC you get private-control-plane and customer-managed KMS. We'll attach our whitepaper.
[09:26] Luis: Sounds good. Can you also share an example of an exponential backoff policy we should use?
[09:31] Maya: Sure — example: base=200ms, multiplier=2, jitter=±30%, attempts up to 4 for interactive flows. For 429s use slower ramp (500ms base) and check rate-limited headers to adapt.
[09:45] Priya: And about partial billing/duplicates — we'll need to reconcile analytics with billing. Can we export raw request logs?
[09:52] Jordan: Yes, exportable via Console or API with timestamps and token counts. We'll include the export schema in the follow-up.
[10:02] Luis: Okay let's summarize next steps.
[10:05] Jordan: Recap: Jordan will send quickstart, cURL/SDK snippets, and the security pack. Maya will create the benchmark plan and a sample harness. Priya will share prompt set and traffic profile. Follow-up: schedule a pilot kickoff the week after materials land.
[10:21] Tom: I'll coordinate calendars. One more question — do you have a recommended client-side rendering heuristic for streaming that balances perceived latency and partial-word issues?
[10:30] Maya: Yes — buffer up to 50ms or until whitespace seen, render then. For very low-latency paths you can show tokens immediately but hide trailing partial characters with a caret. We'll send a 1-page UX guide.
[10:43] Luis: Appreciate it.
[10:45] Jordan: Thanks all. We'll send notes.

End of transcript.
